body: To me this requirement makes no sense. Client-side validation is for UX, not for security. So easily bypassable in web apps it makes very little sense to call it a security control.

comments.body: I agree, calling it a second layer defence I think is wrong.

Consider what can be learned by knowing the client side 'defences' have
been negated, it's not that they are impossible to defeat, it's that they
have been - and that's useful

if the server is receiving data that exceeds the criteria of client side
data that's actionable for security (and troubleshooting)

No ?

@n0x00 I agree this information is useful for anomaly/attack detection, but I wouldn't consider 5.18 (as it's written now) to be about that. I think it is be dangerous to inform developers that you can protect yourself from attacks by implementing security client side (as a secondary defence, but that's an important detail they may not grasp/understand).

This is confusing and is being removed. I do not think anything essential was lost. A new item might be added around using client side sandboxes like DomPurify and JSXSS as part of XSS defense when rendering untrusted HTML. But client slide validation is not something we want to encourage in a security standard.
